Matthew 1.audience: Matthew wrote for readers who knew the Jewish Scriptures, opening with Jesus' descent from Abraham and David (Matthew 1:1). He often notes that events happened "that it might be fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22).

culture.title: Genealogies
culture.text: Matthew arranges the generations in three groups of fourteen. Jewish families kept genealogical records, and the priesthood and royal line depended on them.

culture.title: Betrothal
culture.text: Betrothal was a binding agreement, usually lasting about a year before the couple lived together. Ending it required a formal divorce.

culture.title: Women in the genealogy
culture.text: Four women are named before Mary—Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba ("the wife of Urias")—unusual in a Jewish genealogy.

Matthew 2.audience: Matthew tells of Jesus' birth "in the days of Herod the king" (Matthew 2:1). Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome from 37 to 4 BC.

culture.title: Wise men from the east
culture.text: The magi were scholars and astrologers, probably from Persia or Babylon, who watched the stars for signs.

culture.title: Herod's cruelty
culture.text: Herod killed three of his own sons and his wife Mariamne when he suspected plots. The Roman emperor Augustus is reported to have joked that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son.

culture.title: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh
culture.text: These were costly gifts fit for a king. Frankincense and myrrh were aromatic resins from Arabia and East Africa.

Matthew 3.audience: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness of Judea, and crowds come from Jerusalem and the Jordan region to be baptized (Matthew 3:1–6).

culture.title: Camel's hair and locusts
culture.text: John's clothing recalls Elijah's (2 Kings 1:8). Locusts were a clean food under the law (Leviticus 11:22).

culture.title: Pharisees and Sadducees
culture.text: Pharisees were teachers devoted to strict observance of the law and tradition; Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple.

culture.title: Winnowing fan
culture.text: A winnowing fork tossed grain into the wind to separate wheat from chaff.

Matthew 4.audience: After his temptation, Jesus begins preaching in Galilee and calls fishermen by the Sea of Galilee. Matthew links this to Isaiah 9:1–2.

culture.title: The pinnacle of the temple
culture.text: Herod's temple had a corner at the southeast of the temple mount that towered high above the Kidron valley.

culture.title: Fishing nets
culture.text: Fishermen cast nets from shore or boats and mended them afterward. Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was a family business.

culture.title: Capernaum
culture.text: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee. Remains of a later synagogue and a house venerated as Peter's have been excavated there.

Matthew 5.audience: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) is spoken to the disciples with crowds listening (Matthew 5:1; 7:28).

culture.title: Salt and light
culture.text: Salt preserved food; salt from the Dead Sea contained impurities and could lose its taste. Oil lamps were set on a stand to light the whole house.

culture.title: Jot and tittle
culture.text: The jot (yod) is the smallest Hebrew letter; a tittle is a tiny stroke that distinguishes one letter from another.

culture.title: Going the second mile
culture.text: Roman soldiers could compel civilians to carry their gear for one mile.

Matthew 6.audience: Jesus teaches about giving, prayer, and fasting, and gives the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13).

culture.title: Sounding a trumpet
culture.text: Jesus warns against making a public show of giving to the poor.

culture.title: Moth and rust
culture.text: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing and metal goods, which moths and corrosion could destroy.

culture.title: Lilies of the field
culture.text: Wildflowers covered Galilee's hillsides in spring. Dried grass was used as fuel in clay ovens.

Matthew 7.audience: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the crowds astonished, "for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:29).

culture.title: A mote and a beam
culture.text: A speck of sawdust versus a roof beam—an image a carpenter's son would know.

culture.title: Bread and stone, fish and serpent
culture.text: Bread and fish were the everyday food of Galilee. No father would give his hungry child a stone or a snake instead.

culture.title: Building on rock
culture.text: Winter storms brought flash floods down dry wadis, sweeping away houses built on sand.

Matthew 8.audience: Matthew groups healings and miracles, including a Roman centurion's servant. Jesus says the centurion has greater faith than he has found in Israel (Matthew 8:10).

culture.title: Touching a leper
culture.text: Lepers were ritually unclean and had to live apart (Leviticus 13:45–46). Touching one made a person unclean.

culture.title: A centurion
culture.text: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. Herod Antipas' forces in Galilee were organized on the Roman model.

culture.title: Gadarenes and swine
culture.text: Gadara was a Gentile city of the Decapolis, east of the Sea of Galilee, where pigs were raised.

Matthew 9.audience: Jesus calls Matthew from the tax office (Matthew 9:9)—the Gospel traditionally bears his name—and eats with tax collectors and sinners.

culture.title: Tax collectors
culture.text: Tax and toll collectors worked for Rome or Herod and often charged more than required. They were despised as collaborators.

culture.title: New wine in old wineskins
culture.text: Fermenting wine expands; old, stiff leather skins would burst.

culture.title: Flute players at a funeral
culture.text: Even poor families hired at least two flute players and a mourning woman for a funeral, according to later Jewish tradition.

Matthew 10.audience: Jesus sends out the twelve to "the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matthew 10:6) and warns them of persecution.

culture.title: Shaking off the dust
culture.text: Jews returning from Gentile lands sometimes shook off the dust; doing so to a Jewish town declared it no better than pagan territory.

culture.title: Two sparrows for a farthing
culture.text: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold in the market for food. A farthing (assarion) was a small copper coin.

culture.title: Housetops
culture.text: Flat roofs were used for announcements that could be heard across the village.

Matthew 11.audience: John the Baptist, now in prison, sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who should come. Jesus identifies John as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (Matthew 11:10).

culture.title: Children in the marketplace
culture.text: Children played games of weddings and funerals in the market square.

culture.title: Chorazin and Bethsaida
culture.text: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

culture.title: A yoke
culture.text: Rabbis spoke of taking on ‘the yoke of the law.’ Jesus offers his own yoke as easy.

Matthew 12.audience: Controversies with Pharisees over the sabbath lead them to plot against Jesus (Matthew 12:14). Matthew applies Isaiah 42:1–4 to him (Matthew 12:17–21).

culture.title: Plucking grain on the sabbath
culture.text: Travelers could pick grain by hand from a field (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees counted it as reaping, forbidden on the sabbath.

culture.title: Beelzebub
culture.text: Beelzebub was a name for the prince of demons, from Baalzebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2).

Matthew 13.audience: Jesus teaches the crowds in parables from a boat by the sea (Matthew 13:1–3).

culture.title: Sowing before plowing
culture.text: Farmers scattered seed by hand over fields with paths, rocky patches, and thorns, then plowed it in.

culture.title: Tares
culture.text: Tares are probably darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it ripens and is mildly poisonous.

culture.title: The mustard seed
culture.text: Black mustard seeds are tiny, yet the plant can grow to ten feet tall around the Sea of Galilee.

Matthew 14.audience: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, beheads John the Baptist (Matthew 14:1–12). Jesus then feeds five thousand and walks on the water.

culture.title: Herod's birthday feast
culture.text: The Jewish historian Josephus says John was imprisoned and killed at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea.

culture.title: The fourth watch
culture.text: Romans divided the night into four watches; the fourth was from about 3 to 6 a.m.

culture.title: Baskets of leftovers
culture.text: Jewish custom gathered leftover bread after a meal so that it would not be wasted.

Matthew 15.audience: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem question Jesus about hand-washing. He then travels to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman asks for help (Matthew 15:21–22).

culture.title: Washing hands
culture.text: The "tradition of the elders" required ritual hand-washing before meals—a practice of purity, not hygiene.

culture.title: Corban
culture.text: Declaring property "a gift" (Corban, Mark 7:11) dedicated it to God, which some used to avoid supporting their parents.

culture.title: Dogs under the table
culture.text: Jesus uses the word for small household dogs, and the woman answers with a picture of crumbs falling from the table.

Matthew 16.audience: At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16).

culture.title: Caesarea Philippi
culture.text: Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, had a shrine to the god Pan at a cave and spring, and a temple to Augustus.

culture.title: Keys and binding
culture.text: Keys symbolized authority (Isaiah 22:22). Rabbis spoke of "binding" and "loosing" for forbidding and permitting.

culture.title: Reading the sky
culture.text: ‘Red sky at night’ weather lore was familiar to fishermen and farmers.

Matthew 17.audience: Peter, James, and John see Jesus transfigured with Moses and Elijah. Peter later recalls being with him "in the holy mount" (2 Peter 1:18).

culture.title: Building booths
culture.text: Peter offers to build three tabernacles (booths), like those built for the feast of tabernacles.

culture.title: The temple tax
culture.text: Every Jewish man paid a half-shekel each year for the temple (Exodus 30:13). The coin in the fish's mouth, a stater, paid for two.

Matthew 18.audience: Jesus teaches his disciples about humility, lost sheep, correcting a brother, and forgiveness.

culture.title: A millstone
culture.text: "A millstone" here is a large stone turned by a donkey, far heavier than a hand mill.

culture.title: Ten thousand talents
culture.text: A talent was about 6,000 denarii, twenty years' wages for a laborer. Ten thousand talents was an unpayable sum; the fellow servant owed a hundred denarii.

culture.title: Sold for debt
culture.text: Debtors and their families could be sold into slavery or imprisoned until the debt was paid.

Matthew 19.audience: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan. Pharisees question him about divorce, and a rich young man asks about eternal life.

culture.title: Debates over divorce
culture.text: Rabbis disagreed: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for unfaithfulness, the school of Hillel for almost any cause.

culture.title: A camel through a needle's eye
culture.text: The largest animal in the land through the smallest opening—a picture of impossibility.

culture.title: Blessing children
culture.text: Parents brought children to respected teachers to be blessed by the laying on of hands.

Matthew 20.audience: Jesus tells the parable of the laborers in the vineyard and predicts his death as he goes up to Jerusalem.

culture.title: Day laborers
culture.text: Men waited in the marketplace to be hired for the day. A penny (denarius) was a normal day's wage.

culture.title: The hours of the day
culture.text: The day was counted from sunrise: the third hour was about 9 a.m., the sixth noon, the ninth 3 p.m., and the eleventh 5 p.m.

culture.title: Jericho
culture.text: Jericho was the last town on the pilgrim road from the Jordan up to Jerusalem.

Matthew 21.audience: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:4–5), and drives the money changers from the temple.

culture.title: Hosanna
culture.text: "Hosanna" means ‘save now’ (Psalm 118:25). Pilgrims sang Psalm 118 at the feasts.

culture.title: Money changers
culture.text: Pilgrims exchanged their money for Tyrian shekels to pay the temple tax and bought animals for sacrifice in the temple courts.

culture.title: Leasing a vineyard
culture.text: Absentee landowners leased vineyards to tenant farmers for a share of the harvest.

Matthew 22.audience: In the temple courts, Pharisees, Herodians, and Sadducees each try to trap Jesus with questions.

culture.title: Tribute to Caesar
culture.text: The denarius bore the image of the emperor Tiberius and called him the son of the divine Augustus—offensive to many Jews.

culture.title: A wedding garment
culture.text: Guests were expected to come properly dressed to a wedding feast.

culture.title: Sadducees and resurrection
culture.text: The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses as binding and denied the resurrection.

Matthew 23.audience: Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples against the scribes and Pharisees and pronounces woes on them.

culture.title: Phylacteries and borders
culture.text: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding Scripture passages worn on the forehead and arm. Borders are the tassels on garments (Numbers 15:38).

culture.title: Moses' seat
culture.text: A stone seat for the teacher has been found in ancient synagogues, such as at Chorazin.

culture.title: Whitewashed tombs
culture.text: Tombs were whitewashed before Passover so pilgrims would not touch them by accident and become unclean.

Matthew 24.audience: On the Mount of Olives, Jesus foretells the destruction of the temple. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

culture.title: The temple stones
culture.text: Herod's temple was built of huge white limestone blocks; some in the retaining walls weigh many tons.

culture.title: Fleeing from the housetop
culture.text: Outside stairs led from flat roofs to the street, so one could flee without going into the house.

culture.title: A fig tree's leaves
culture.text: Fig trees are bare in winter and leaf out in late spring, signaling summer.

Matthew 25.audience: Jesus continues his teaching on the Mount of Olives with parables of the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats.

culture.title: Wedding processions
culture.text: The bridegroom came at night to bring the bride to his home; attendants with lamps escorted the procession.

culture.title: Talents
culture.text: A talent was a large sum of silver, many years' wages. The English word ‘talent’ comes from this parable.

culture.title: Sheep and goats
culture.text: Mixed flocks grazed together by day; shepherds separated them at night, since goats needed more warmth.

Matthew 26.audience: Matthew recounts the plot against Jesus, the Last Supper at Passover, Gethsemane, and the trial before the high priest Caiaphas.

culture.title: Alabaster ointment
culture.text: Precious perfumes were kept in sealed alabaster jars; the neck was broken to pour it out.

culture.title: The Passover meal
culture.text: Passover was eaten in Jerusalem with roasted lamb, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, and cups of wine, reclining at the table.

culture.title: Caiaphas
culture.text: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36. An ossuary inscribed ‘Joseph son of Caiaphas’ was found in Jerusalem in 1990.

Matthew 27.audience: Jesus is tried before Pontius Pilate, crucified, and buried in Joseph of Arimathaea's tomb.

culture.title: Pontius Pilate
culture.text: Pilate was Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. A stone inscription with his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

culture.title: Crucifixion
culture.text: Romans reserved crucifixion for slaves, rebels, and violent criminals. The condemned carried the crossbeam, and a placard stated the charge.

culture.title: A rock-cut tomb
culture.text: Wealthy families cut tombs into rock, sealed with a large stone rolled across the entrance.

Matthew 28.audience: The Gospel ends with the resurrection and Jesus sending his disciples to "teach all nations" (Matthew 28:19).

culture.title: The guard at the tomb
culture.text: The tomb had been sealed and guarded (Matthew 27:66). The guards shake with fear, and the chief priests later pay them to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15).

culture.title: Women as first witnesses
culture.text: In Jewish courts of the time, women's testimony was given less weight, yet women are the first to find the empty tomb.
